title: Certified synthesis of system-scale programs from reviewable specifications

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a synthesizer that takes a compact, reviewable formal specification and produces both a substantial systems program and a machine-checkable proof that the program implements the specified behavior. An independent checker would validate the proof. The input would describe required behavior precisely while leaving substantial implementation choices to the synthesizer. Program synthesis already has the underlying goal of finding programs that satisfy specifications; this concept adds a demanding combination of system scale, specification compactness, human reviewability, independently checked correctness and practical performance.

Conceptual synthesis: a file-system specification might define permitted operations, observable results and crash behavior while leaving data structures, storage layouts and recovery mechanisms open. The synthesizer would resolve those choices and prove that the resulting implementation refines the specification: its modeled behavior remains within what the specification permits. The intended input is already formal enough to support that proof. Establishing that it expresses stakeholder intent and adequately models the operating environment belongs to SWE-03.

This target cannot be distinguished from current work simply by saying that existing tools verify code while the proposed tool generates it. Anthropic's October 2026 report includes a generated and verified interpreter. The relevant question is whether a demonstration combines substantial scale with a genuinely compact, auditable specification, independent proof checking and useful performance. The supplied evidence does not settle whether that complete combination has been achieved.

significance.text: Conditional impact synthesis: achieving this capability could make the reviewed formal specification the main artifact engineers maintain, while automating substantial implementation and proof work. For protocols, storage systems, schedulers and compiler components, this could remove considerable work on representations, error paths and concurrency mechanisms wherever the specification leaves those choices open. Changes to required behavior could then drive regeneration of a conforming implementation rather than repeated manual reconstruction of implementation details.

The assurance would be stronger than evidence from successful tests alone, but would remain bounded by the actual theorem. Behavior excluded by the proved specification would be ruled out within the modeled scope, conditional on sound checking components and semantics. Deployment would also need to preserve the correspondence between the checked artifact and the running program. A proof does not establish that the specification captures reality, and a partial-correctness proof does not by itself establish termination. Anthropic's reported interpreter result illustrates this distinction: it establishes agreement with formal semantics whenever the interpreter returns.

Conditional impact synthesis: the analogy with compilation is useful because both processes turn a higher-level artifact into executable detail. Here, however, the specification may permit many implementations, and the synthesizer must choose among them while producing evidence of conformance. The potential revolution is removal of a large avoidable gap between a reviewable behavioral description and working code. Essential problem complexity remains; some requirements cannot be compressed much further. This does not imply universal synthesis, elimination of human decisions, competitive performance in every domain or automatic generation of a specified share of all software. Wider adoption and downstream productivity gains would require separate evidence.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target capability is the reliable integration of program search, implementation construction and proof production at substantial systems scale. Gulwani, Polozov and Singh's 2017 survey identifies ambiguity of user intent and the enormous space of possible programs as inherent synthesis challenges. Its account of successful applications in particular domains motivates the target, but neither establishes the present-day absence of the proposed combination nor shows that restricted-domain synthesis cannot itself transform engineering practice.

Engineering synthesis: a compact specification must leave enough freedom to avoid reproducing the implementation, yet constrain behavior sufficiently for a meaningful proof. The synthesizer must select representations, algorithms and mechanisms whose interactions satisfy that specification. For concurrent or failure-prone systems, the specification and proof must explicitly address whichever scheduling, communication, persistence and failure behaviors fall within the guarantee. A short specification cannot earn its compactness by hiding essential decisions in uncounted libraries, scaffolding or informal assumptions.

Proof generation must also scale without making the independently checked evidence impractically expensive. The Verus publication abstract reports 6.1K implementation lines and 31K proof lines across its case studies, illustrating that verification artifacts can be much larger than the implementation. That aggregate does not measure synthesis difficulty directly, but it shows why automatically producing usable implementations and their proofs is a substantial combined objective.

Engineering synthesis: correctness, synthesis cost and runtime performance must be reconciled. A system that eventually discovers a conforming but unusably slow implementation would satisfy only part of the target. Failure reporting is another barrier: an unsuccessful search may reflect insufficient resources or inability to construct a proof, rather than an impossible specification or a missing human decision. The tool must expose these different outcomes without claiming more than it has established.

current_state.text: The retained OpenAIRE abstract identifies Program Synthesis by Gulwani, Polozov and Singh, dated 11 July 2017, DOI 10.1561/2500000010, in Foundations and Trends in Programming Languages 4(1–2):1–119. It describes synthesis as automatically finding a program satisfying intent expressed through a specification, identifies intent ambiguity and a large program search space as challenges, and reports industrial deployment of programming-by-examples applications. Only the abstract is available in the supplied review; the publisher page was not captured. These findings provide historical context rather than a complete account of the November 2026 frontier.

The retained publication abstract for Verus: A Practical Foundation for Systems Verification, listed with a November 2024 venue entry, reports case studies totaling 6.1K implementation lines and 31K proof lines, or roughly five proof lines per implementation line in aggregate. This supports the significance of verification effort. The landing-page abstract does not establish the sizes of relational specifications or the proportions of implementation and proof written by humans, so those stronger claims cannot be retained as demonstrated findings.

Anthropic's 22 October 2026 report describes checked no-crash proofs for 239 entry points across 123 OSS-Fuzz libraries, for inputs up to 64 MB. The reported scope includes assertions and is conditional on stated assumptions, including a single-threaded, static RISC-V/Linux execution model. It concerns selected entry points rather than complete functional correctness of whole libraries. The report describes generated proofs checked against specifications, including checking by the Rocq kernel, but the proofs were not supplied for independent rechecking in this review.

The same report and its appendix describe generating a Rust interpreter for a Python fragment, completing all 17 tiers of the reported task and proving agreement with formal semantics using Verus. The theorem is partial correctness: whenever the interpreter returns, its result agrees with those semantics. Correspondence between the formal semantics and CPython was tested empirically. This is relevant progress in generating verified code, so a blanket claim that language-model-generated code is uncertified would be misleading. The supplied evidence does not establish the interpreter's specification-to-implementation size ratio, specification review time or comparative runtime performance, and therefore does not establish that it meets this concept's combined criteria. The appendix's awkward whitespace extraction did not prevent the reviewer from reading these distinctions.

The research attributes substantial specification-writing effort and unfavorable annotation-inference comparisons to Lathouwers and Huisman's May 2024 Survey of annotation generators for deductive verifiers. Its text was not retained in the supplied review, so the detailed claims about minority coverage of a human baseline and Daikon annotations being mostly unnecessary or wrong remain unverified here. Likewise, the retained IronFleet item is a GitHub viewer shell without paper text; it cannot substantiate claims about specification compactness, proof volume or human authorship. These access limitations do not establish that the attributed findings are false.

The research also attributes to Brun and coauthors' September 2026 roadmap a separation of requirements elicitation, source-code synthesis and proof synthesis, with their integration remaining a research challenge. The roadmap text was not captured, so that attribution cannot be independently supported by the supplied review. Separately, the supplied freshness-search record is empty. Consequently, the evidence establishes several relevant achievements and limitations, but does not establish whether the complete proposed capability remained undemonstrated as of 1 November 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: fix a formal specification that a skilled engineer can read and audit in one day, then have the synthesizer produce a substantial file system, consensus implementation or compiler pass together with a refinement proof accepted by a checker independent of the synthesizer. Record the review procedure and what the reviewer understood, including assumptions and permitted behaviors. The input must already be formal enough to refine; deriving an adequate specification from stakeholder language remains a separate SWE-03 task. These are proposed evaluation choices, not established standards.
completion_criteria.label: One-day-auditable spec yields independently checked substantial systems refinement proof

completion_criteria.text: Proposed compactness and performance criteria: the specification should be at most about one tenth of the generated implementation's length under a declared counting convention. Account explicitly for imported definitions, supplied implementation scaffolding and other material that could conceal essential complexity. Require runtime performance within a declared small factor of a named, respected handwritten implementation on stated workloads. The ratio and performance factor are proposed thresholds, and the baseline, hardware, configurations and measured resource use must be disclosed.
completion_criteria.label: Spec at most one tenth implementation, small factor handwritten runtime

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and assurance criteria: release the fixed specification, generated implementation, proof artifacts, tool versions and checking instructions so independent parties can rerun proof checking and performance measurements. Document supported languages, synthesis resources, manual interventions, trusted checking components, formal semantics and environmental assumptions. State whether the proof covers termination, functional results, crashes, concurrency, persistence or other properties, and show how the checked artifact corresponds to the evaluated executable. Repeated generation runs should report success rates and resource costs rather than only a selected success.
completion_criteria.label: Proof and performance reruns report assurance, success rates and costs

completion_criteria.text: Proposed failure and breadth criteria: report a checked impossibility result only within its declared language or search space, request a missing decision when one has been identified, and explicitly allow inconclusive outcomes such as resource exhaustion or inability to prove a candidate correct. Reproduce the result on several materially different systems tasks to demonstrate breadth. Finite successes would establish capability across those tasks and assumptions, not literal universality or a guarantee that every valid specification can be synthesized.
completion_criteria.label: Breadth on several materially different systems tasks, scoped failure claims

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis — SWE-01, Push-button verifying compilation for practical systems: both seek automatically checked assurance for practical code. SWE-01 centers on verifying compilation and implementation correctness; SWE-02 additionally asks the tool to construct the substantial implementation from a compact behavioral specification. They share checking infrastructure, while imposing different demands on program generation.

Roster-based synthesis — SWE-03, Demonstrable adequacy of a specification against intent and the environment: SWE-02 begins with a formal specification suitable for refinement. SWE-03 addresses whether that specification expresses the intended behavior and sufficiently captures the environment. Success at synthesis cannot substitute for adequacy, and adequacy alone does not produce an implementation.

Roster-based synthesis — SWE-04, A compositional calculus for concurrent systems that fail: such a calculus could supply specifications and proof rules for synthesizing systems with concurrency and failures. SWE-04 concerns reasoning compositionally about those behaviors; SWE-02 concerns constructing programs that satisfy the resulting specifications.

Roster-based synthesis — SWE-05, Assurance that stays proportional to each behavioral change: maintaining specifications and regenerating implementations could create demand for efficient incremental assurance. SWE-05 addresses the cost of preserving assurance after changes; SWE-02's initial generation and proof capability does not by itself establish proportional update costs.

Roster-based synthesis — SWE-06, Sound behavioral recovery of legacy systems: recovered legacy behavior could help inform a specification for subsequent synthesis. The distinction is direction: SWE-06 recovers behavior from an existing system, while SWE-02 constructs an implementation from a supplied specification. Recovery also does not automatically establish that the recovered behavior is desirable.

Roster-based synthesis — SWE-07, Practical confinement of general untrusted programs: confinement could be a specified property of generated software or an operating boundary around it. SWE-07 targets restrictions on untrusted execution; SWE-02 targets construction of implementations with checked conformance. A proof of confinement would cover only one part of a broader behavioral specification.

Roster-based synthesis — SWE-08, Sequential meaning for fault-tolerant distributed execution: a sequential behavioral model could give a synthesizer a compact target for a distributed implementation. SWE-08 concerns providing that meaning under distributed faults; SWE-02 would additionally need to construct and certify an implementation against it.

Roster-based synthesis — SWE-09, Observable determinism as the default for parallel systems code: determinism could simplify the observable behavior that a generated parallel system must satisfy. SWE-09 concerns the execution model and programming guarantees; SWE-02 concerns generating implementations and proofs, whether the specification requires determinism or permits nondeterminism.

Roster-based synthesis — SWE-10, Proof-carrying behavioral composition across trust boundaries: synthesized components could carry proofs used when they are combined with other components. SWE-10 addresses assurance across composition and trust boundaries. A proof that one generated component refines its specification does not alone establish that a larger assembly satisfies its obligations.

Roster-based synthesis — SWE-11, Proved semantics-preserving transformation of practical systems: verified transformations could optimize a synthesized implementation while retaining its established behavior. SWE-11 begins with a program whose semantics must be preserved; SWE-02 begins with a specification that may admit many implementations. Their proof machinery could overlap without making the advances identical.

unresolved_issues: Whether any demonstration available by 1 November 2026 meets the combined scale, specification compactness, reviewability, independent-checking and performance criteria remains unresolved because no freshness searches were supplied.
The reported interpreter's specification-to-implementation ratio, specification review burden, comparative performance and full checking trust boundary are not established by the supplied review.
The reported OSS-Fuzz proofs were not supplied for independent rechecking; the record supports the dated report rather than a fresh replication.

The annotation survey's detailed baseline and Daikon findings, IronFleet's specification and proof characteristics, and the Brun roadmap's attributed decomposition remain unverified from the retained materials.

A useful counting convention for specification compactness, treatment of shared libraries and scaffolding, and a concrete acceptable performance factor still need to be chosen for an actual evaluation.

A one-day specification review and a finite set of systems tasks would require a defined review protocol and task-selection rationale; neither would establish universal auditability or synthesis capability.

brief.title: Software built from clear rules, with proof it follows them
possible: Engineers could maintain a short, precise description of how software must behave and have a tool build the working program, choosing its internal design. The tool would also produce a mathematical proof that the program follows those rules, checked by a separate program.
why: For software that stores files, coordinates computers or translates code, this could automate much of the implementation and proof work. Changes to required behavior could lead directly to a rebuilt program, reducing the details engineers must reconstruct by hand.

sources.showed: They proved selected software could not crash under specified conditions. They also generated a program that runs a subset of Python and proved its results follow formal rules whenever it returns.
sources.quote: Using Claude, we proved security properties at the assembly code level (RISC-V) in over 100 real-world open-source software libraries.
sources.cited_for: AI can generate both working code and checked proofs of specified behavior.
sources.not_established: The generated program's rule length, review effort and comparative speed remain unclear; its proof does not guarantee it finishes.

sources.showed: Their Verus tool checked proofs for varied systems software. Across the examples, proof code was roughly five times longer than implementation code.
sources.quote: Verus verifies code 3–61x faster and with less effort than the state of the art.
sources.cited_for: Checking systems software can require much more proof code than implementation code.
sources.not_established: These examples do not establish automatic construction of substantial programs and proofs from short, reviewable rules.

sources.showed: IronFleet concerns proving practical distributed systems correct.
sources.cited_for: It concerns correctness proofs for systems that coordinate computers.
sources.not_established: It does not establish automatic program generation from compact rules.

sources.showed: This research roadmap addresses integrating requirements gathering, code generation and proof generation.
sources.cited_for: It addresses the integration needed to build software with correctness guarantees.
sources.not_established: A research roadmap does not demonstrate the complete capability.

sources.who: Sumit Gulwani, Oleksandr Polozov and Rishabh Singh
sources.showed: Their survey describes automatic program construction from stated requirements, including commercial tools that build programs from examples.
sources.quote: In the last decade, several applications of synthesis in the field of programming by examples have been deployed in mass-market industrial products.
sources.cited_for: Automatic program construction already works in particular application areas.
sources.not_established: Those applications do not establish substantial systems software built from compact rules with checked proofs and practical speed.

sources.showed: This survey examines tools that generate annotations, the supporting statements used to prove software correct.
sources.cited_for: It addresses automation of statements needed for software proofs.
sources.not_established: Generating supporting statements alone does not establish automatic construction of a complete program and proof.

shown: Anthropic reports generating a program that runs a subset of Python and proving that its answers follow precise mathematical rules whenever it returns. This combines code generation with a correctness proof.
Anthropic and Theorem also report checked proofs against crashes across selected parts of 123 software libraries. Those guarantees depend on a restricted execution model and cover specified behavior.
missing: A substantial program built from short, reviewable rules, with its proof accepted by an independent checker.
Practical running speed without hiding essential design choices in supporting code or assumptions.
Repeatable generation across different systems tasks, with clear success rates, costs and explanations of unsuccessful attempts.

milestones.label: A substantial program proved against rules reviewable within a day
milestones.explanation: An engineer would have to audit the formal rules in one day, and a separate checker would accept proof that a generated systems program follows them. This would connect human review to independently checked behavior.

milestones.label: Short rules and competitive running speed
milestones.explanation: The rules would have to be at most one tenth the program's length, counting hidden supporting material, while speed stays within a declared small factor of a respected handwritten program. This would test compactness and usefulness.

milestones.label: Repeatable proof checks, performance results and generation costs
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to repeat proof checks and speed measurements, with assumptions, human help and repeated generation outcomes disclosed. This would establish what the guarantee covers and how reliably it can be obtained.

milestones.label: Success across different tasks and honest failure reports
milestones.explanation: Results would have to span materially different systems tasks, separating proved impossibility, missing decisions and inconclusive searches. This would establish breadth without treating every unsuccessful attempt as impossible.

uncertain: Whether any demonstration combines substantial scale, short reviewable rules, independent proof checking and useful speed remains unresolved.
How should rule length count shared libraries and supporting code, and what performance gap is acceptable?
A proof guarantees only the modeled behavior; it does not establish that the rules capture real needs or that the program always finishes.

page.title: Proof-producing synthesis of systems software
page.definition: A synthesizer constructs a systems program from an expert-reviewed formal behavioral specification and produces a proof that its modeled behavior satisfies that specification. The specification leaves implementation choices open; a checker separate from the synthesizer checks the proof.

goal.need: A 2018 study found 10 previously unknown recovery bugs in widely used Linux file systems. Some could cost users files already written to disk. Crash tests exercise a bounded set of workloads. A proof can cover every crash the specification describes, but the expert labor is substantial: the correctness proof specific to the seL4 kernel took 11 person-years. Generating code and proof together could put such guarantees within reach of more systems teams. The guarantee depends on the specification capturing how the hardware behaves.

figures.caption: Implementation and proof artifacts in the Verus systems case studies
figures.note: Aggregate counts across the reported case studies; these do not measure human effort.

statements.body: DARPA, High-Assurance Cyber Military Systems programme
statements.quote: HACMS seeks a synthesizer capable of producing a machine-checkable proof that the generated code satisfies functional specifications

statements.body: Yuriy Brun, Saikat Chakraborty, Claire Le Goues, Corina Păsăreanu and Adish Singla, Automatically Engineering Trusted Software: A Research Roadmap
statements.quote: automatically synthesizing formal proofs to verify the correctness of the produced software
statements.context: The roadmap pairs this goal with generating source code from formal specifications that express users’ intent.

completion.title: Independent checking establishes refinement for a complete synthesized systems program.
completion.criterion: Generate a complete systems program and a functional-refinement proof from a fixed, expert-reviewed behavioral specification. Refinement means every modeled implementation behavior is permitted by the specification, including its specified progress and failure behavior. Cover the selected system's full public interface and failure model. The specification leaves algorithms and data representations open; imported assumptions and libraries are included in review. A separate checker accepts the proof, and the evaluated executable is connected to the proved artifact. The executable meets workload and resource constraints specified before synthesis.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; proposed integrated demonstration rather than an externally established completion threshold.
completion.basis: Searched HACMS goals, the trusted-software roadmap, and Fiat, IDS and Vero evaluations for a combined test of systems scope, specification compactness, human review and runtime performance; none supplied one. This proposal retains their shared synthesis-and-proof objective without assigning numerical compactness or review-time limits. Vero reports 27 of 43 repositories fully solved by its strongest configuration, but its endpoint does not establish executable performance.

milestones.title: An imperative routine and a proof of its input-output behavior and loop termination are synthesized.
milestones.criterion: Given an input-output specification, permitted atomic operations, a loop template, stack limits and bounds on specified operations, synthesize an imperative routine within those constraints. Synthesize loop invariants establishing partial correctness and ranking functions establishing termination. The generated guards and statements must be well formed.
milestones.set_by: Srivastava, Gulwani and Foster, published proof-theoretic synthesis formulation in From Program Verification to Program Synthesis.
milestones.threshold_quote: partial correctness, loop termination, and well-formedness conditions on program guards.

milestones.title: A synthesized data structure has a refinement proof accepted by the Coq kernel.
milestones.criterion: Refine a declarative specification of an abstract data type, a set of operations on private state, into a functional implementation. Produce a proof that the implementation’s operations satisfy the specification and that Coq’s kernel accepts. The implementation checked at this stage is the functional program represented in Coq.
milestones.set_by: Fiat developers, using the established proof-assistant convention of kernel acceptance for refinement proofs; the published demonstration concerns query structures.
milestones.threshold_quote: Each refinement process leaves a proof trail, checkable by the normal Coq kernel, justifying its soundness.

milestones.title: Synthesized, linked assembly satisfies its original high-level specification.
milestones.criterion: Produce a fully linked assembly program represented as a term in Coq. Coq must check a proof that this linked program satisfies the original high-level specification, including calls to any separately verified routines linked into it.
milestones.set_by: Pit-Claudel and colleagues, foundational refinement and linking criterion in Extensible Extraction of Efficient Imperative Programs with Foreign Functions, Manually Managed Memory, and Proofs.
milestones.threshold_quote: a fully linked assembly program represented as a Coq term with a proof that it meets the original high-level specification.

milestones.title: A synthesized distributed store passes proof, audit and execution checks in at least 2 of 3 runs.
milestones.criterion: For one fixed distributed key-value-store specification, at least two of three independent synthesis runs must succeed. Each successful run must close the refinement proof in Rocq without unproved placeholders, pass the benchmark audit for a non-vacuous implementation of the specified interface, and execute the extracted OCaml implementation on the distributed test harness. A run that exhausts its time or cost budget fails.
milestones.set_by: IDS benchmark authors, Section 5.1 and Table 1; the published cutoff and execution tests concern distributed key-value-store specifications.
milestones.threshold_quote: Rocq Qed accepted, audit step passed, extracted OCaml runs on the harness

milestones.title: Every scored interface in a Vero instance is implemented and every specification is proved in Lean 4.
milestones.criterion: Starting from one curated Vero project in code-and-proof mode, supply a function body for every scored interface and a Lean 4 proof of every scored specification against those implementations. The grader must accept the submission after inserting the permitted edits into a fresh benchmark copy and checking proof dependencies against its allowed axioms.
milestones.set_by: Vero benchmark authors, code-and-proof mode and grading rules in section 3.2.
milestones.threshold_quote: implement every API and prove every specification against its own implementations.

not_found: No external completion test was located that jointly bounds specification compactness, human review effort, systems scope and runtime performance.
No programme or academy assessment was found that judges proof-producing synthesis for a specified systems program unachievable or unworthy of pursuit.

results.finding: Claude proved no crashes for 239 OSS-Fuzz entry points across 123 libraries.
results.detail: When Claude patched code, the specification was regenerated from the patched executable. The reported proofs therefore establish the no-crash property for the resulting binaries under the modeled conditions.
results.quote: Claude successfully patched the bugs it found and then proved that there are no crashes on any input (up to 64 MB) for 239 entry points across 123 different OSS-Fuzz libraries.

results.finding: VS3 synthesized integer square root with a loop invariant and ranking function in a median of 9.96 seconds across three runs.
results.detail: Source type is coded as report because the available kinds omit conference proceedings. The source is a peer-reviewed POPL conference paper.

results.finding: Fiat synthesized functional implementations with Coq-checked refinement proofs for 3 query ADTs.
results.detail: The supplied text identifies itself as a submission and gives no publication venue. Confirmation rests on the Coq-checked refinement proof.
results.quote:
In contrast, derivations of ADTs with
Fiat are completely veriﬁed by Coq, and these derivations may be
integrated within larger, more general proof developments.

results.finding: Fiat applied Coq-certified functional ADT synthesis to 6 example programs.
results.detail: The proof covers the Gallina implementation. The paper separately reports OCaml extraction and benchmarking for Messages and Classiﬁer. The supplied manuscript refers to an anonymous supplement and gives no publication venue.

results.detail: The checked assembly artifact is Bedrock. The translator to x86, assembler, and wrappers are part of the trusted base.
results.quote: The pipeline runs entirely within the Coq proof assistant, leading to final, linked assembly code with overall full-functional-correctness proofs in separation logic.

results.finding: IDS passed the proof, audit, and execution checks in 3/3 independent runs for Chapar causal consistency.
results.detail: The pass count comes from Table 1. Rocq checks the refinement proof, while the audit, execution, and repeat-run outcomes are empirical results reported by the authors.

results.finding: IDS passed 176/189 VERINA tasks requiring both a function body and a Lean 4 proof.
Sepref generated imperative LLVM code with correctness and complexity proofs in 2 case studies.
results.detail: Sepref translates the abstract algorithm’s existing control flow and uses user hints where needed to discharge proof obligations.
results.quote:
• We extend the Sepref tool (Section 4) to synthesize executable imperative code in LLVM,
together with a proof of correctness and complexity.

results.finding: The dynamic-array case study verifies 1 operation, push, through a functional refinement with amortized constant cost.
results.detail: The case study verifies push and discusses how the method could extend to lookup, update, initialization, and destruction.
results.quote:
We verify the amortized-constant-time push operation of
dynamic arrays in the abstract NREST formalism and then synthesize LLVM code from it using
the automatic method from the previous section.

results.finding: Introsort refinement reaches generated LLVM for 2 element types, unsigned integers and strings.
results.detail: The string instantiation bounds comparison cost using the maximum string length. Compilation to machine code is outside the checked refinement.
results.quote:
Finally, instantiating the element type and comparison operation yields a complete LLVM
program, that our code generator can translate to actual LLVM text and a corresponding header
file for interfacing our sorting algorithm from C or C++.

results.finding: Rupicola generated 1 in-place ASCII uppercasing routine with a Coq proof of total correctness.
results.detail: The user supplied the functional model, the calling interface, and compilation hints. Bedrock2 tracks stack usage, but the example does not give a stack budget or bounds on specified operations as synthesis inputs.
results.quote:
The result is a Bedrock2 program upstr_br2fn and its
proof of (total) correctness upstr_br2fn_ok (the Derive
command is syntactic sugar for defining a dependent pair).

results.finding: The paper names 1 IP-checksum example with an end-to-end proof and describes a verified route from the generated Bedrock2 code to RISC-V.
results.detail: The performance experiments used C pretty-printing and conventional C compilers. Verified linking is described as a toolchain capability.
results.quote:
Still, expressivity is a
concern, so for multiple of our example programs we wrote
end-to-end proofs connecting abstract specifications to Rupi-
cola’s inputs.

results.finding: AxDafny verified 56.4% of synthesized solutions across 250 LCB-Pro-Dafny tasks.
results.detail: The verifier checked individual solutions. The aggregate success rate is an author-reported benchmark result.
results.quote:
On the newly introduced LCB-Pro-Dafny benchmark, AxDafny verifies 56.4% of tasks, improving over the 11.6%
success rate of direct GPT-5.5 generation.

results.finding: JetStream generated accelerators with Verus-checked answer correctness for all 22 TPC-H queries.
results.detail: The checked limits on when an operation may decline do not establish loop termination.
results.quote: The accelerator’s data structures, query execution, and maintenance logic are all verified.

results.finding: JetStream’s generated auxiliary data structures have contracts checked in Verus for 3 operations per accelerator.
results.detail: The operation proofs assume the host supplies scans, deltas, and rescans that satisfy the declared input contracts.
results.quote: The accelerator’s data structures, query execution, and maintenance logic are all verified.

results.finding: GPT-5.5 (xhigh) fully solved 27 of 43 Vero projects in code-and-proof mode.
results.detail: On deposit_sc, one of the accepted projects, Lean checked all 79 scored specifications across four modules against the submitted implementations.
results.quote: Our evaluation shows that Vero is frontier-resistant, as the strongest configuration fully solves only 27 of 43 instances in code-and-proof mode and 10 instances resist every configuration in both modes.

results.finding: One statically linked RISC-V cryptographic server satisfies its high-level I/O specification under one end-to-end Coq theorem.
results.detail: The theorem assumes the verified code is loaded at the specified entry address, the initial I/O trace is empty, and the required memory is available.
results.quote:
the complete software image compiled with Bedrock2,
certified with one Coq theorem about a machine-code sequence.

goal.need = "A 2018 study found 10 previously unknown recovery bugs in widely used Linux file systems. Some could cost users files already written to disk. Crash tests exercise a bounded set of workloads. A proof can cover every crash the specification describes, but the expert labor is substantial: the correctness proof specific to the seL4 kernel took 11 person-years. Generating code and proof together could put such guarantees within reach of more systems teams. The guarantee depends on the specification capturing how the hardware behaves.". Reason: The proof-line count measures artifact size, while the kernel study measures labor and the storage study identifies a consequence for users.

add statement by Yuriy Brun, Saikat Chakraborty, Claire Le Goues, Corina Păsăreanu and Adish Singla, Automatically Engineering Trusted Software: A Research Roadmap, 2026: "automatically synthesizing formal proofs to verify the correctness of the produced software". Reason: The trusted-software roadmap explicitly names both code synthesis and proof synthesis as goals.

edit m1: title = "An imperative routine and a proof of its input-output behavior and loop termination are synthesized."; criterion = "Given an input-output specification, permitted atomic operations, a loop template, stack limits and bounds on specified operations, synthesize an imperative routine within those constraints. Synthesize loop invariants establishing partial correctness and ranking functions establishing termination. The generated guards and statements must be well formed."; threshold_quote = "partial correctness, loop termination, and well-formedness conditions on program guards."; threshold_ref = 7. Reason: The criterion needs to require the synthesized proof and distinguish its obligations from the paper’s example programs.

edit m2: criterion = "Refine a declarative specification of an abstract data type, a set of operations on private state, into a functional implementation. Produce a proof that the implementation\u2019s operations satisfy the specification and that Coq\u2019s kernel accepts. The implementation checked at this stage is the functional program represented in Coq.". Reason: The Fiat criterion mixes the kernel’s acceptance test with a case-study result and subsequent OCaml compilation.

edit m3: criterion = "Produce a fully linked assembly program represented as a term in Coq. Coq must check a proof that this linked program satisfies the original high-level specification, including calls to any separately verified routines linked into it."; threshold_quote = "a fully linked assembly program represented as a Coq term with a proof that it meets the original high-level specification."; threshold_ref = 8. Reason: The linked-assembly theorem identifies the precise artifact checked by Coq, which the existing criterion obscures with case-study details.

edit m4: criterion = "For one fixed distributed key-value-store specification, at least two of three independent synthesis runs must succeed. Each successful run must close the refinement proof in Rocq without unproved placeholders, pass the benchmark audit for a non-vacuous implementation of the specified interface, and execute the extracted OCaml implementation on the distributed test harness. A run that exhausts its time or cost budget fails.". Reason: The distributed-store criterion mixes the per-specification pass rule with the observed success count and runtime measurements.
